The paper introduces TIDMAD, a comprehensive time-series dataset and benchmarking suite derived from the ABRACADABRA-10cm dark matter experiment. The proposed dataset includes ultra-long 10 MS/s time series with hardware-injected calibration signals that emulate expected dark matter signatures and provides two benchmarking metrics: a denoising score based on spectral SNR and a dark matter limit benchmark that directly translates denoising performance into physics-constrained detection capabilities. The paper bridges machine learning and experimental physics, offering a valuable resource to advance AI-driven discovery in fundamental science.

The paper received positive reviews, including one strong accept, with consensus among reviewers that TIDMAD represents a novel and impactful contribution. The dataset is high quality, well-documented, and reproducible, and the proposed benchmarks provide a unique link between machine learning performance and physics discovery potential. The work is well-motivated and clearly presented, making it accessible to both ML practitioners and physicists.

Some concerns were raised by reviewers, including:
(a) dataset specificity to ABRACADABRA-10cm and its generalizability to other detectors,
(b) usability of the second benchmark, which involves a full frequentist likelihood analysis and may be challenging for ML researchers,
(c) limited science run duration (~24 hours), which constrains standalone sensitivity,
(d) segmentation of deep learning models by frequency and limited generalization across the full frequency range,
(e) benchmarking restricted to higher-amplitude (50 mV) injections without extensive coverage of weaker 10 mV signals,
(f) concerns regarding dataset representativeness and potential environmental bias in data collection,
(g) insufficient details on classical baseline hyperparameter selection and model size comparisons, and
(h) justification for using machine learning over traditional denoising techniques.

The authors provided comprehensive rebuttals and additional experiments addressing these issues. They clarified the dataset’s portability and ongoing collaborations with other experimental teams (DMRadio, ADMX, HAYSTAC), provided supporting results for generalizable architectures such as WaveNet, explained the rationale behind amplitude selection, and benchmarked traditional signal processing methods and Fourier averaging, showing that ML models substantially outperform them. Further, they included hyperparameter sweeps for classical baselines, provided model size details, and justified the necessity of ML-based denoising given the complex, non-Gaussian nature of real detector noise.

The AC finds strong support from the reviewers to merit the paper for publication. The dataset and benchmarks provide a significant resource to bridge machine learning and fundamental physics, enabling reproducible and impactful research. It is highly encouraged for the authors to incorporate reviewer feedback in their final revision, particularly clarifying the usability of Benchmark-2 and highlighting the potential for extending TIDMAD to broader experimental collaborations.

===== FINAL UPDATE FROM DB Track PCs ====

The final decision for this paper has been taken by the program chairs after consultation with the SACs. All Senior Area Chairs have ranked papers according to the feedback from the AC during the review process. We decided to leave the original meta-review to reflect the opinion of the AC in light of the initial discussions with reviewers and SAC.

Dear Reviewers and Area Chair,

Thank you for the valuable time you invested in reviewing this paper. On behalf of all authors, we believe your comments have helped make this paper much better. Below is a summary of the rebuttal process:

After the rebuttal, all reviewers have recommended acceptance of this paper. The rebuttal process supports our claim that TIDMAD is the first AI-ready dataset from a real dark matter search capable of producing publication-grade physics results. All reviewers (BGs7, oPwg, YqoJ, 1TXv) highlighted that the dataset is generated from a real dark matter detector with high relevance to fundamental physics. The majority of the reviewers (BGs7, oPwg, YqoJ) praised TIDMAD's high quality, capability to bridge the gap between ML and fundamental physics communities, and the novelty of the two proposed benchmarking metrics. Specifically, Reviewer oPwg considered TIDMAD "a rare and valuable opportunity to apply ML for fundamental physics discovery." Additionally, all reviewers (BGs7, oPwg, YqoJ, 1TXv) acknowledged that the manuscript is well-organized, clear, and easy to understand even for non-physicists, with Reviewer oPwg specifically praising the excellent reproducibility, comprehensive documentation, and good accessibility of this dataset.

Several limitations and weaknesses have been clarified and addressed during the rebuttal period. One concern was the motivation for using machine learning (raised by Reviewer 1TXv) for TIDMAD and the need for traditional benchmarking methods. We clarified this through additional studies and presented evidence showing that only machine learning algorithms can efficiently denoise the TIDMAD dataset. Multiple reviewers brought up questions about the choice of injected signal amplitude and frequency. We clarified that both signal amplitude and frequency are unknown parameters in dark matter searches. In response, we also conducted additional experiment on weaker signal amplitudes. Reviewer oPwg pointed out the limitation of frequency splitting (i.e., training multiple models to handle different frequency ranges) and suggested WaveNet and multiresolution transformers to enhance generality. We benchmarked the WaveNet model on TIDMAD and found that indeed a single trained model could denoise across all frequency ranges. Additional concerns such as run limitations, broad applicability, and Gaussian noise are all carefully clarified and addressed. 

After the rebuttal, Reviewers YqoJ and 1TXv commented that most of their concerns and misunderstandings were addressed; they increased their scores to suggest acceptance of this paper, while Reviewer BGs7 maintained their original acceptance recommendation and Reviewer oPwg maintained their strong support for acceptance.

Thank you again,

Authors

Thank you for your thoughtful and detailed review. We’re grateful that you found the writing clear and accessible, and we appreciate the opportunity to clarify several points you raised.

# 1. Missing Figure
Thank you for noting that Figure 6 in the appendix was referenced but not displayed correctly. We have fixed this issue in the updated version of the manuscript.

# 2. Motivation for Using Machine Learning
While the dark matter signal is expected to appear as a sinusoid, its frequency is not known a priori. The frequency corresponds directly to the unknown mass of the dark matter particle, and as outlined in **Section 1.1** and **Appendix A**, this frequency spans several orders of magnitude. As such, applying a traditional Fourier Transform or bandpass filter tailored to a known frequency is not feasible — it risks filtering out the very signal we hope to detect.

|:------------:|:-------------:|:------------------:|:------------:|:--------------:|

| Moving Average | 3040 | - | -1.23 | -1.14 |
| Moving Average | 3810 | - | -1.23 | -1.14 |
| SG Filter | 19 | 11 | 0.95 | 1.04 |
| SG Filter | 171 | 5 | 0.58 | 0.69 |
| SG Filter | 945 | 2 | -0.41 | -0.31 |
| SG Filter | 405 | 5 | 0.30 | 0.42 |
| SG Filter | 1245 | 15 | -2.77 | -2.35 |

**Table A:** Fine and coarse denoising score for Moving Average and Savitzky–Golay filter under different parameters

The benchmarking result we showed in the paper and additional studies show that **only machine learning algorithms can efficiently denoise the TIDMAD time series**. We summarize our supporting evidence below.

- As shown in Table 1 of the original manuscript, raw TIDMAD time series without any denoising has its _Benchmark 1: fine denoising score_ equal to 1. Higher denoising score means better performance. All tested traditional algorithms produce a denoising score below 1, while all machine learning algorithms produce a denoising score above 1.
- We conducted additional study with 60 trials of moving average and SG filter algorithms under different hyper parameters, and the results are displayed in Table A. Notably, none of the 60 trials surpassed the baseline denoising score of 1.0 achieved when no denoising algorithm is applied. Moreover, the best-performing hyperparameter configurations represents an extreme under-regularized scenario. For example, the best-performing SG configuration uses a 11-dimensional polynomial to fit a 19 sample window, essentially memorizing and preserving all raw time series features. This demonstrates that the tested traditional methods are fundamentally inadequate for handling the complex noise characteristics within the TIDMAD dataset, as they can at best only asymptotically approximate the raw time series without providing meaningful denoising improvements. 
- Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we tested Fourier Averaging which was originally adopted by the ABRACADABRA experiment. For every 10-second time series segment, a Fourier transform is applied to each one-second interval, and the resulting 10 Fourier spectra are averaged to produce a single spectrum representing the 10-second segment.  This method yields a fine denoising score of 0.243 — still worse than 1. This result is shown in Table B.
- Following the suggestion of other reviewers, we benchmarked two additional deep learning algorithms (RNN Seq2Seq and WaveNet). As shown in Table B, both achieve denoising scores greater than 1.0.

We believe these pieces of evidence strongly support our paper’s claim that machine learning is necessary for denoising the TIDMAD dataset, given that it offers flexible denoising across a wide frequency range without presupposing the signal location in frequency space. This flexibility is crucial in the context of dark matter detection, where the signal frequency is an open parameter to search for.

| Algorithms | Segment Size | FS | Parameters | Fine Score | Coarse Score |
|:------------:|:--------------:|:----:|:-----------:|:------------:|:--------------:|
| None | | | | 1.00 | 1.10 |
| Fourier Averaging | 1×10⁸ | N/A | 10-fold Average | 0.24 | 0.26 |
| Moving Average | 1×10⁶ | N/A | window = 100 | 0.86 | 0.95 |
| SG Filter | 1×10⁶ | N/A | window = 19, order = 11 | 0.95 | 1.04 |
| FC Net | 4×10⁴ | Yes | See Appendix A2 | 6.43 | 6.55 |
| PU Net | 4×10⁴ | Yes | See Appendix A2 | 3.69 | 3.84 |
| Transformer | 2×10⁴ | Yes | See Appendix A2 | 3.95 | 4.18 |
| WaveNet | 4×10⁴ | No | See Appendix A2 | 4.99 | 5.16 |
| RNN Seq2Seq | 4×10⁴ | Yes | See Appendix A2 | 3.38 | 3.79 |

**Table B:** Fine and coarse denoising score for raw data, traditional algorithms, and trained ML models. FS means frequency splitting, or training multiple versions of the same model to handle different frequency ranges. The detail of segment size and FS is discussed in Section A2. **FS=No** means a single model is trained to handle all frequencies.

# 3. Comparison to Traditional Methods
The original manuscript provides comparison to traditional moving average and SG filter denoising algorithms. Additionally, we have added Fourier Averaging (explained in 2.) as another traditional baseline. Fourier averaging has been used by ABRACADABRA to report its past physics results. This approach effectively suppresses phase-incoherent noise but has limited ability to address phase-coherent noise. When evaluated using our Benchmark 1 denoising score, this averaging method yields a coarse score of 0.255 and a fine score of 0.243—substantially lower than the performance achieved by our ML models. We will include these results explicitly in our revised manuscript.

# 4. Model Selection and Frequency Learning
We agree and acknowledge in the original manuscript that a fully connected network (FCN) achieved the best performance is somewhat surprising. Following the reviewer's suggestion, we benchmarked an RNN sequence-to-sequence model, a classical approach for sequential data denoising. The results are shown in Table B, with fine denoising score of 3.38, which falls below FCN's score of 6.43. Following Reviewer oPwg’s suggestion, we benchmarked the WaveNet model which was originally designed for audio generation. WaveNet produced a fine denoising score of 4.99, closer to FCN. 

We believe that with further architectural development, sequential model approaches could eventually outperform FCN. However, the central scope of this paper is the TIDMAD dataset and two specifically designed benchmarking metrics. We are careful not to imply that FCN is the optimal architecture; rather, we present it as a baseline and hope this dataset will encourage the development of more sophisticated models that can surpass FCN's performance to better search for dark matter.

**Regarding frequency learning, because the signal frequency is unknown and variable, the model cannot be expected to directly learn a single fixed frequency.** We will revise the manuscript to make this point more explicit.

# 5. Nature of the Noise and Use of Synthetic Data
We appreciate your concern about the role of Gaussian noise. The injected Gaussian noise is used solely to validate our scoring metric in controlled experiments. In practice, the actual detector noise is highly non-Gaussian, as can be seen in the PSD shown in Figure 2. We will revise line 214 to clarify that while Gaussian noise is used for certain validation studies, the primary data remains real and contains complex, non-Gaussian structure. This complexity is essential for benchmarking ML methods under realistic conditions, and cannot be adequately captured by synthetic Gaussian data alone.

---
Once again, we thank you for your insightful comments. We will incorporate these clarifications and corrections into the next version of the paper.

Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive review. We appreciate your recognition of the dataset's novelty, our evaluation metrics, and your careful attention to details that will help strengthen this work. We address each of your concerns in turn.
# 1. Justification of Signal Amplitudes
The amplitudes of the injected synthetic signals (50 mV and 10 mV) were selected to balance realism with detectability. Because the strength of a true dark matter signal is an open question in theory, we cannot fix its amplitude a priori. As detailed in Appendix A, the 50 mV amplitude was chosen to ensure detectability using traditional signal processing techniques, which we relied on to establish ground truth for our benchmark scores. Although smaller amplitudes would simulate weaker electromagnetic couplings and pose an interesting ML challenge, they would fall below the threshold of traditional methods, making them unusable as supervised labels in our current framework.

To support further research, we also provide a secondary dataset with 10 mV signals across the same frequency range (1.1 kHz – 4.9 MHz). While these data were not used in training or benchmarking, they are publicly available and can serve as a resource for researchers interested in low-SNR scenarios. We benchmarked the fully connected network (FCN) on the 10mV signals, and obtained a denoising score of 4.61 (Fine) and 4.63 (Coarse). As a reference, the FCN denoising score for 50mV signal is 6.43 (Fine) and 6.55 (Coarse) as shown in Table 1 of the manuscript.

# 2. Environmental Noise and Generalizability
We acknowledge that our dataset was collected on a single ABRA detector in a specific laboratory environment. However, the denoising framework—including the data split protocol, signal injection methodology, and evaluation metrics—is readily transferable to other axion dark matter experiments that utilize similar hardware and calibration techniques. We are actively collaborating with teams from DMRadio, ADMX, and HAYSTAC, all of which yield a similar time series data structure with voltage-vs-time readout and hardware injection.

Due to the expense and technical constraints of these experiments—including dilution refrigerators operating below -272.1 Celsius and large superconducting magnets (>1 Tesla) — data collection is currently limited to a small number of detectors. Constructing a new detector would require multi-million-dollar investments. However, ongoing efforts in cross-lab benchmarking and noise modeling will improve generalizability, and we view this dataset as a first step in a broader collaborative framework.

# 3. Classical Method Parameter Selection
Thank you for highlighting this important point. In response to your comment, we designed 60 experimental trials to systematically evaluate the hyperparameters of moving average and Savitzky–Golay filter:
- Moving Average (10 trials): Window size randomly sampled from the range [10, 5000]
- Savitzky–Golay filter (50 trials): Window size randomly sampled as odd numbers from [11, 2001], and polynomial order randomly sampled from [2, 20]

The result of this study is shown in the table below.

| None | | | 1.00 | 1.10 |
| Moving Average | 19 | - | 0.86 | 0.95 |
| Moving Average | 99 | - | 0.56 | 0.69 |
| Moving Average | 100 | - | 0.52 | 0.64 |
| Moving Average | 622 | - | -0.31 | -0.47 |
| Moving Average | 974 | - | -0.57 | -0.47 |
| Moving Average | 1169 | - | -0.61 | -0.72 |
| Moving Average | 2632 | - | -1.07 | -0.97 |

We found that the fine denoising scores across all tested configurations ranged from -2.5 to 1.0. Both algorithms showed improved performance with smaller window sizes: Moving Average achieved its best fine denoising score of 0.86 with a window size of 19, while Savitzky-Golay filter performed optimally with small window sizes and low polynomial orders, reaching its peak score of 0.95 using window size 19 and polynomial order 11. 

Notably, this best-performing SG configuration represents an extreme under-regularized scenario where an 11-dimensional polynomial is fitted to every 19 elements, essentially memorizing and preserving all time-series features. Critically, none of the 60 trials surpassed the baseline denoising score of 1.0 achieved when no denoising algorithm is applied. This shows that traditional signal processing methods are fundamentally inadequate for handling the complex noise characteristics within the TIDMAD dataset, as they can at best only asymptotically approximate the raw time series without providing meaningful denoising improvements. These findings underscore the necessity of deep learning-based approaches for effective denoising in this challenging dataset.

We agree it was premature to draw strong conclusions prior to this study, and we have added these results to the updated manuscript as a new appendix E.

# 4. Deep Learning Model Sizes
We agree that model complexity is a key factor in comparing architectures. Details regarding the number of layers, parameters, and training time for all three deep learning models are included in Appendix B of the manuscript. We apologize if this section was not clearly referenced in the main text and will ensure it is more prominently cited in the revision.

---
We thank you again for your insightful comments, which have led to several improvements in the manuscript. We hope these clarifications and updates address your concerns.

Thank you for your thoughtful review and strong support. We sincerely appreciate your recognition of this dataset’s novelty, scientific potential, and cross-disciplinary accessibility. We are also grateful for your insightful suggestions, which we address below:

# 1. Limited Science Run Duration
We agree that the 24-hour science run, while representative, limits the absolute sensitivity achievable with this dataset. The ABRA detector is a shared facility, and our access to extended runtime is subject to broader scheduling constraints. That said, a positive reception to this work could help motivate further dedicated data-taking campaigns. 

# 2. Frequency-Specific Deep Learning Models
Thank you for the suggestion to investigate more generalizable architectures. Motivated by your comment, we designed a simple WaveNet model trained on the full frequency range of data and benchmarked it on the TIDMAD dataset. The result is posted in the following table.
| Algorithm         | Segment Size | FS   | Parameters               | Fine Score | Coarse Score |
|-----------------------|----------------|------|-------------------------------|:-------------:|:---------------:|
| None             | N/A             | N/A  | N/A                      | 1.00           | 1.10             |
| Fourier Averaging| 1×10⁸           | N/A  | 10-fold Average          | 0.24           | 0.26             |
| Moving Average   | 1×10⁶           | N/A  | window = 100             | 0.86           | 0.95             |
| SG Filter        | 1×10⁶           | N/A  | window = 19, order = 11  | 0.95           | 1.04             |
| FC Net           | 4×10⁴           | Yes  | See Appendix A2          | 6.43           | 6.55             |
| PU Net           | 4×10⁴           | Yes  | See Appendix A2          | 3.69           | 3.84             |
| Transformer      | 2×10⁴           | Yes  | See Appendix A2          | 3.95           | 4.18             |
| WaveNet          | 4×10⁴           | No   | See Appendix A2          | 4.99           | 5.16             |
| RNN Seq2Seq      | 4×10⁴           | Yes  | See Appendix A2          | 3.38           | 3.79             |

**Table Caption:** Fine and coarse denoising score for raw data, traditional algorithms, and trained ML models. FS means frequency splitting, or training multiple versions of the same model to handle different frequency ranges. The detail of segment size and FS is discussed in Section A2. **FS=No** means a single model is trained to handle all frequencies.

WaveNet achieved denoising scores of 4.99 (Fine) and 5.16 (Coarse) on Benchmark 1, ranking second only to the fully connected network. Remarkably, WaveNet is the only model that does not rely on FS (i.e., training multiple models for different frequency ranges); instead, a single WaveNet model is trained to denoise across all frequencies. We believe WaveNet represents an extremely promising avenue for ABRACADABRA and plan to investigate it further.

# 3. Use of 10 mV Data in Benchmarks
You are correct that our current benchmark does not incorporate the 10 mV signal injections. As described in Appendix A, it is a convention of the ABRACADABRA experiment to choose 50mV. At amplitudes as low as 10mV, the signal is not consistently discernible above the detector noise, making it infeasible to calculate ground truth SNR values across the full frequency range. This ground truth SNR is necessary to calculate our Benchmark-1 denoising score.

While we did not include 10 mV data in our training or benchmarking, we have released it publicly to support future work in low-SNR regimes. We also benchmarked the fully connected network (FCN) on the 10mV signals, and obtained a denoising score of 4.61 (Fine) and 4.63 (Coarse). As a reference, the FCN denoising score for 50mV signal is 6.43 (Fine) and 6.55 (Coarse) as shown in Table 1 of the manuscript.

# 4. Discovery Potential and Scope
We fully agree that the dataset and framework can enable true discovery-level analysis. However, in this paper, we deliberately focused on dataset creation and benchmarking to ensure clarity and accessibility, particularly for the ML community. A discovery analysis would require integrating detailed physics priors and likelihood modeling, which we felt might obscure the core ML contributions. That said, the authors are actively pursuing this direction in a follow-up work, including toy discovery pipelines built atop this denoising benchmark.

---
Once again, thank you for your support and high-confidence recommendation. We look forward to incorporating these improvements into the final version of the manuscript.

Thank you for your careful and encouraging review. We are glad that you found the dataset, benchmarks, and manuscript well-organized and scientifically valuable. We would like to address the two limitations you raised:
# 1. Dataset Specificity to ABRACADABRA-10cm
You are correct that the dataset is based on the ABRACADABRA-10cm experiment and reflects the specific hardware and noise environment of that detector. However, the overall framework—including the injection protocol, data splits, and evaluation benchmarks—is intentionally designed to be portable. We are currently collaborating with other teams from DMRadio, ADMX, and HAYSTAC, which also yield similar time-series data structures and use hardware signal injections to understand their detector. Because the denoising and benchmarking methods are detector-agnostic, we believe this approach can be generalized to a broad class of axion dark matter experiments. This work lays the groundwork for such generalization, and we hope the paper will encourage similar releases from other experimental collaborations.

# 2. Usability of Benchmark-2 for ML Researchers
We appreciate your concern that the second benchmark—based on a full frequentist likelihood analysis—may appear daunting to researchers without a background in physics. We would like to point out that this frequentist likelihood analysis is widely accepted by the physics community to report dark matter results, and has been adopted by ABRACADABRA to report its past physics results. 

To facilitate easy production of Benchmark 2, we designed the accompanying software tools to abstract away the underlying complexity. Users do not need to engage directly with the physics assumptions or statistical computations; instead, they can input the denoised time-series produced by their model into a provided script, which then computes the dark matter limit in a reproducible and physics-valid way.

We consider Benchmark 2 one of our key novelties, as it allows AI/ML experts to directly produce a physics result. Our goal is to make scientifically meaningful benchmarking accessible to the ML community without sacrificing physical rigor. We will revise the manuscript to make this plug-and-play functionality of Benchmark-2 more explicit.

---

summary.value:
The paper presents TIDMAD, a novel time-series dataset generated by the ABRACADABRA-10cm dark matter experiment. It includes:
1. Training data with hardware-injected synthetic dark matter-like signals,
2. Validation data for benchmarking denoising performance, and
3. Science data for setting real dark matter detection limits.

The authors introduce two key benchmarks:
- A denoising score based on signal-to-noise ratio in the frequency domain,
- A dark matter limit benchmark, using standard particle physics analysis to assess how denoising enhances detection sensitivity.

This dataset bridges machine learning and experimental physics, enabling ML methods to produce results meaningful in fundamental science.

strengths_contributions.value:
- Significant scientific impact: This is the first ML-ready dataset capable of yielding real, publication-grade dark matter search limits (Section 4.2). It is a rare and valuable opportunity to apply ML for fundamental physics discovery.
- Novel benchmarking methodology: The introduction of a denoising score grounded in spectral SNR (Eq. 7, Section 4.1) and a dark matter limit (Figure 5) connects ML performance directly to physical constraints on dark matter candidates.
- High-quality dataset: Ultra-long 10 MS/s time series are rare in open data. The authors provide:
- Precise signal injection aligned with theoretical models (Appendix A),
-- Channel-synchronized ground truth vs. noisy readout for supervised denoising (Section 1.2),
--Well-documented HDF5 files and reproducible scripts.
-- Baseline models and reproducibility: Traditional and DL models (moving average, SG filter, FC-Net, PU-Net, Transformer) are trained, benchmarked, and their code is made available. FC-Net achieves the best denoising score (6.43, Table 1).
- Clear and organized presentation: The manuscript is accessible to both physicists and ML practitioners. Figures (e.g., Figures 1–7) are well-captioned and informative.
- Generalization potential: Applicable to other dark matter searches (e.g., ADMX, HAYSTAC) and denoising tasks in seismology, ECG, gravitational waves (Section 5).

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- Limited science data duration: The 24-hour science run is only ~1% of ABRA Run 3, limiting the standalone sensitivity (Section 5). While the denoised limit improves by 1–2 orders of magnitude, it does not outperform prior runs.
- Segmented DL models: The need to train four frequency-specialized models (Appendix B) reveals limitations in model generalization across the full frequency range.
- Suggestion: Investigate multi-scale or hybrid models (e.g., WaveNet, multiresolution transformers) to enhance generality.
- Denoising benchmarks limited to injected signals: Although weak-injection data (10 mV) is available, only 50 mV signals were used in benchmark development. This constrains evaluation under lower SNR regimes.
- Suggestion: Include weak-injection data in benchmarking or simulate signals at realistic noise thresholds for broader utility.
- Discovery potential not fully explored: While the framework enables science-level searches, discovery analysis is deferred to future work (Section 5). Some reviewers may consider this a missed opportunity.
- Suggestion: Consider including toy discovery examples using the framework.

The dataset is
- Publicly accessible via GitHub and OSDF.
- Provided in .hdf5 format with conversion factors, channel definitions, and scripts for training/inference/benchmarking (Section 2, Figure 3).
- Trained model weights are shared via a public Google Drive link (Appendix B).

final_justification.value:
I recommend 6: Strong Accept for the following reasons:
1. Resolved Concerns
- The authors clarified the scope of the science run and justified its duration, noting that the dataset’s primary purpose is to enable benchmarking rather than outperform prior ABRA runs.
- They addressed model generalization concerns by adding preliminary multi-frequency model results (App. C), showing feasibility beyond the four-segment approach.
- They confirmed that weak-injection data will be included in a future benchmark release, mitigating concerns about SNR coverage.
2. Key Strengths Maintained
- This is the first ML-ready dataset capable of producing real, publication-grade dark matter search limits, bridging ML and experimental physics.
- The two benchmarks—spectral SNR denoising score and dark matter limit—directly link ML performance to physical discovery potential, a rare and impactful design choice.
- The dataset is high-quality, fully documented, and reproducible, with accessible code, scripts, and model weights.
- Presentation remains exemplary, accessible to both physics and ML audiences.
3. Remaining Minor Limitations
- Model generalization to the full frequency range still requires further exploration, though initial results are promising.
- Discovery-level analysis is deferred to future work, which slightly limits immediate physics output but is reasonable given the dataset’s benchmarking focus.

Overall, the submission combines scientific novelty, strong technical rigor, and high community utility, making it a valuable resource for both ML and fundamental physics communities. The remaining limitations do not detract from its significance.

summary.value: This work provides a realistic time-series dataset that is used for dark matter detection algorithm development, which is essentially an inverse problem on 1-D signal under extremely low SNR. Given the dataset, the recovory performance is benchmarked on several approahces that includes both classical (signal-processing based) algorithm and deep-learning models.

strengths_contributions.value:
- It seems like this is the first ever dataset that is collected for dark matter signal estimation (recovery).
- The proposed evaluation metrics seems to be novel.
- The benchmarked performance could be informative to future research on this problem.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
I appreciate the authors' approach to collecting a dataset by injecting artificial sinusoidal signals, as it is indeed challenging to obtain clean dark matter signals. However, this raises concerns about ensuring the collected dataset is unbiased and representative of real-world data distributions containing true dark matter signals. Specifically, I would like to question the choice of two amplitude values (50 mV and 10 mV) for the injected signals in the training data. Are these values representative of expected amplitudes in real dark matter signal scenarios? If so, by any chance that we can provide any justification or clarification. If not, why were these specific values chosen? Is it due to limitations in generating other voltages, or is the recovery process insensitive to amplitude?

Similarly, as the dataset was collected on a single machine in a specific lab environment, I wonder if the noisy signal distribution might be influenced by the environment. If similar data were collected in a different setting, how would this potential mismatch in data distribution affect the performance of the recovery algorithm?

Regarding the performance benchmarking on several algorithms, including classical methods (moving average and Savitzky-Golay filter) and deep learning models, the hyperparameters for the classical methods (e.g., window size of 100) are presented without justification. This may lead to an unfair comparison with the deep learning-based model if the parameters were chosen heuristically rather than through careful selection based on a training subset.

Furthermore, the three deep learning models are described without providing information on their sizes or complexities. This lack of detail makes it difficult to interpret the results, particularly the conclusion that the FC Net has the best performance. A fair comparison requires consideration of model sizes and complexities to ensure that the results are meaningful and informative.

Overall, while the proposed dataset collection method is understandable, it is essential to address these concerns to ensure the validity and generalizability of the results.

summary.value: This work introduces a dataset derived from the ABRA-10 experiment, which is used to detect dark matter signals. The task is framed as a sequence-to-sequence problem: the output is a sinusoidal wave of a single frequency, and the input is a combination of random noise and the output signal—essentially making this a denoising task. The authors evaluate several machine learning architectures on this dataset, including FC nets, PU nets, and Transformers.

strengths_contributions.value:
* The dataset is sourced from real sensor measurements, providing a degree of realism and practical relevance.
* The writing is clear and accessible, even for readers without a background in physics or dark matter detection.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Figure 6 is referenced in the text but is missing.

2. **Motivation for Using Machine Learning**:
   * The task involves recovering a sinusoidal signal with a single dominant frequency. It’s unclear why machine learning is necessary here.
   * A traditional signal processing approach such as Fourier Transform should be able to extract the dominant frequency effectively. What are the limitations of such traditional methods in this context?
   * What is the performance of the best-known non-ML method on this task? Including such a baseline is essential to justify the need for ML methods.

3. The best-performing model is a fully connected network, which is not inherently designed for sequential data. This is unexpected, considering the sequential nature of the task. Can we just let the model to learn the frequency?

4.  Line 214 mentions that the noise follows a Gaussian distribution. If the distribution of the noise is know, then the value of collecting real sensor data becomes questionable. Could a synthetic dataset generated using Gaussian noise serve the same purpose?

title.value: TIDMAD: Time Series Dataset for Discovering Dark Matter with AI Denoising

TLDR.value: TIDMAD is the first dataset and benchmark from a dark matter physics experiment, providing ultra-long time series data and comprehensive benchmarking tools that enable models to directly advance the fundamental physics search for dark matter.

abstract.value: Dark matter makes up approximately 85\% of total matter in our universe, yet it has never been directly observed in any laboratory on Earth. The origin of dark matter is one of the most important questions in contemporary physics, and a convincing detection of dark matter would be a Nobel-Prize-level breakthrough in fundamental science. The ABRACADABRA experiment was specifically designed to search for dark matter. Although it has not yet made a discovery, ABRACADABRA has produced several dark matter search results widely endorsed by the physics community. The experiment generates ultra-long time-series data at a rate of 10 million samples per second, where the dark matter signal would manifest itself as a sinusoidal oscillation mode within the ultra-long time series. In this paper, we present the TIDMAD --- a comprehensive data release from the ABRACADABRA experiment including three key components: an ultra-long time series dataset divided into training, validation, and science subsets; a carefully-designed denoising score for direct model benchmarking; and a complete analysis framework which produces a physics community-standard dark matter search result suitable for publication as a physics paper. This data release enables core AI algorithms to extract the dark matter signal and produce real physics results thereby advancing fundamental science.

pdf.description: Upload your submission as a PDF file that ends with .pdf. In this file the main text (max. nine pages), references, and checklist may be followed by technical appendices, for which there is no page limit. Paper PDF can be updated until the full paper submission deadline (May 15).

dataset_submission.description: Indicate whether your submission includes a dataset. **If you check this box, you must provide a valid Croissant metadata file and a URL to your dataset accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** For detailed requirements, please refer to the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines).

croissant_file.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, upload a Croissant metadata file that documents your dataset. If your submission has more than one Croissant metadata file, please package all files into a single ZIP archive and upload it here. **Before uploading, verify that your file is valid using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/JoaquinVanschoren/croissant-checker).** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**

enum.description: We acknowledge the responsible reviewing obligations as authors.
